transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-08
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Oakridge Head of Platform), Tom Suarez (Oakridge ML Eng), Lina Park (Oakridge SecOps)

Summary:
Quick POC sprint planning focused on integrating Redwood via an SDK adapter into Oakridge's telemetry pipeline. Goals: define success criteria (latency & accuracy), agree workload sizing and benchmark plan, confirm whether Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) will be used for pilot, and outline SDK/function-calling/structured-output integration steps. Security & compliance checklist to be shared.

Topics covered:
- Workload profile (QPS, tokens per request, burst patterns)
- Success criteria and pass/fail thresholds (latency, throughput, output quality)
- Benchmark design and timeline
- Integration approach: Redis-like KV cache vs Redwood prefix caching, SDK adapter, OpenAI-compatible endpoints and function/tool calling, structured JSON output schema
- Security: SOC2, KMS/HSM, SSO, VPC/Private deployment considerations

Action items (captured in metadata) and next steps summarized at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then we want to run through the pilot scope — looking to set concrete success metrics and the benchmark plan. Ethan will cover the tech bits.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hi all, Priya here. We're trying to replace a portion of our summarization/alert enrichment flow that currently hits a public LLM. Cost and latency have ballooned as we ramp devices. We'll need to see both perf and cost improvements.
[00:30] Tom Suarez: Tom from ML. We have three workloads: 1) short anomaly summaries (~30-80 tokens output, ~40-120 token context), 2) classification/rerank on candidate alerts (embeddings & rerank), and 3) an interactive triage chat for ops (~150-300 tokens). Peak concurrent requests hit ~180 qps for the summarization stage during regional bursts.
[00:53] Lina Park: SecOps — we will need details on data residency and whether logs go out to a public plane. SOC2 is a must, and KMS integration for keys.
[01:10] Ethan Ross: Great, thanks. Quick note: Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For a pilot we usually recommend Dedicated if you want predictable p99 SLAs and isolation; Private if you need full network isolation or an air-gapped setup. Hosted is fastest to get started but less isolation.
[01:40] Priya Nair: Our security bar is pretty high — we prefer VPC but we can compromise on Dedicated with an outbound-only egress policy if needed.
[01:50] Maya Chen: Noted. Let's capture success criteria — what are you targeting for latency and accuracy?
[01:58] Tom Suarez: For the summarization endpoint: p95 < 220ms and p99 < 400ms for a 256-token context/response profile. For rerank, throughput matters more — want to process ~2k embedding lookups per minute with <100ms average per embedding call. Also cost target: reduce current 60% unit cost vs what we're paying now.
[02:25] Ethan Ross: Okay that's helpful. We'll map model families and batching configs. A few practical items for the benchmark: we need representative request traces (timestamps, token counts, concurrency patterns), and sample payloads so we can reproduce tokendistribution.
[02:45] Priya Nair: We can extract traces — we'll send last 72 hours of anonymized telemetry. Expect many short requests and some long contexts for root-cause threads.
[02:58] Maya Chen: Thanks. On integration, did you want to use OpenAI-compatible endpoints or the Redwood SDK directly?
[03:05] Tom Suarez: Prefer to keep the code changes minimal — OpenAI-compatible endpoints with our existing wrapper would be ideal, and then we can swap in a native SDK adapter later for advanced features like function calling and caching.
[03:18] Ethan Ross: That makes sense. Redwood's OpenAI-compatibility layer supports function/tool calling semantics and structured output. Caveat: some advanced batching/kv cache hooks require the SDK or slight changes to the call flow to expose streaming and partial KV reuse.
[03:36] Lina Park: Can you describe KV cache? We've heard the term K-V cash a few times in vendor docs, just want clarity.
[03:43] Ethan Ross: Sure — sorry if docs called it KV cash, it's KV cache: Redwood can persist prefix key/value states (embedding or attention caches) between requests to reduce repeated compute across similar sessions. For telemetry, we use prefix caching and token reuse heuristics — it reduces per-token amplifier costs in stable-dialog flows. For stateless summarization there is less gain, but for the triage chat it helps.
[04:05] Tom Suarez: Sounds useful for the triage chat. For summarization we mostly need low tail latency.
[04:12] Maya Chen: For the pilot I suggest a two-phase benchmark: Phase A = OpenAI-compat smoke + latency profile on Hosted or Dedicated; Phase B = SDK-enabled run with KV caching and batching on the same model family to measure unit cost delta. Each phase includes a scripted 2-hour load run plus regressions on 50 representative prompts.
[04:34] Priya Nair: Timeline wise, if you can run the first smoke by 2/15, we could start integrating and run the SDK phase the following week. Our internal sprint wraps 2/21 so we'd like results before that.
[04:46] Maya Chen: We can do that. Ethan, can you outline what you need to prepare the benchmark?
[04:51] Ethan Ross: We'll need: 1) Anonymized traffic traces (Priya), 2) Representative payloads for each workload (Tom), 3) Target SLAs and pass/fail thresholds (Priya/Tom), 4) Credentials for a test account (we'll generate a scoped API key), 5) Network details if you want a Private or Dedicated deployment for the run (Lina). We'll supply a benchmark runbook and a scripts repo.
[05:18] Priya Nair: We will provide traces and a sandbox project in our AWS account for the Dedicated run. For VPC we need to know if Redwood supports customer-managed route tables and hub-spoke designs.
[05:29] Ethan Ross: Redwood Private supports VPC peering and private link; you can control route tables on your side. For Dedicated we do a managed subnet approach but can restrict egress. We'll send a diagram.
[05:39] Lina Park: Please include an ingress/egress diagram plus what logs are captured and retained. Also, our compliance team needs to know if any cleartext payloads transit Redwood control plane.
[05:49] Maya Chen: We'll include that in the SOC2 + network notes. Also, KMS — do you use customer-managed keys?
[05:56] Lina Park: Yes, prefer CMK in AWS KMS; if Redwood supports external HSM or bring-your-own-key that's ideal.
[06:03] Ethan Ross: We integrate with AWS KMS for private deployments and offer HSM options for on-prem. For Hosted there's envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys but you can opt for CMK with Dedicated.
[06:17] Tom Suarez: Side question — function calling. We use a small internal enrichment service (IP lookup, device metadata). Ideally the model should return a structured JSON with fields that map to our enrichment tool inputs, so we can call it automatically.
[06:31] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We can define a JSON schema for the structured response and use function/tool calling pattern to ask the model to return a structured payload. Redwood's structured output validators can enforce shape during inference if you run SDK mode.
[06:44] Tom Suarez: Will there be any behavior difference between OpenAI-compat endpoint function-calling and native SDK?
[06:50] Ethan Ross: Functionally similar, but the SDK exposes more hooks: pre-send token cost estimation, KV cache control, and streaming partial structured outputs which we use to shorten tail p99s. OpenAI-compat works fine for basic function calls.
[07:04] Priya Nair: For cost modeling, how do you recommend we size Dedicated capacity? We have diurnal spikes and weekly big dumps when regions sync.
[07:13] Ethan Ross: We'll run the benchmarks to estimate steady-state throughput and peak QPS. For Dedicated you can reserve baseline GPUs and enable burst capacity. Typically we'd recommend sizing to 80% of your 95th percentile and enable autoscale for the top 5-10%. We'll give a sizing matrix after Phase A.
[07:30] Maya Chen: To be precise, please send: 1) 95th and 99th percentile requests per minute for each workload, 2) average tokens in/out, 3) acceptable p50/p95/p99 latency targets and cost per 1k tokens target. We'll map that to model families and quantization profiles for the POC.
[07:48] Priya Nair: We'll provide those by tomorrow EOD.
[07:52] Tom Suarez: Regarding quality, we want a small eval set of 150 prompts with human labels to check regressions. Can you run quality monitors and diff outputs across models?
[08:02] Ethan Ross: Yes, Redwood Optimize supports eval-based regression checks. For the POC we can run side-by-side comparisons and provide metrics (BLEU-ish, ROUGE, task-specific accuracy) and sample outputs.
[08:14] Lina Park: For auditability, how long do logs live and who can access them? We need at least 90 days retention and RBAC on logs.
[08:23] Ethan Ross: Default retention is 30 days for hosted logs, but we have enterprise retention options (90/365d) and RBAC integrated with your SSO. We'll include log retention and access controls in the SOW.
[08:37] Maya Chen: OK, let's capture the pilot timeline: Week 1 (2/8-2/14): onboarding, exchange traces and access, run Phase A smoke by 2/15. Week 2 (2/15-2/21): Phase A full 2-hour benchmark and initial sizing. Week 3 (2/22-2/28): SDK integration and Phase B benchmark with KV caching. Week 4: analysis & decision. Is that aligned?
[08:57] Priya Nair: That looks doable; the key dependency is our infra team clearing the sandbox for the Dedicated run.
[09:05] Maya Chen: We'll send the SOW and pilot pricing matrix tomorrow. Any immediate concerns?
[09:12] Tom Suarez: Just one more — can we get sample SDK snippet for function calling in Node and Python? That would accelerate the integration.
[09:19] Ethan Ross: Yes, we'll attach two small samples and an adapter template to drop into your wrapper.
[09:24] Lina Park: Also include docs about tokenization differences — our tooling assumes OpenAI tokenization and we've hit mismatches before.
[09:32] Ethan Ross: Good call — we'll highlight any tokenizer differences and recommend a small acceptance test.
[09:37] Maya Chen: Alright recapping next steps: Maya sends SOW + pricing + SOC2 + network diagram; Ethan sends benchmark runbook, SDK adapter samples, and initial sizing worksheet; Priya/Tom send traces, payloads, and targets; Lina confirms KMS vendor and VPC constraints. We'll schedule the benchmark window for week of 2/15.
[09:58] Priya Nair: Thanks — we'll aim to get artifacts by 2/10.
[10:02] Tom Suarez: Thanks everyone. Looking forward — we'll prioritize the representative prompts.
[10:07] Maya Chen: Great. I'll follow up with calendar invites and a shared repo link. End of call.

Notes about transcription: occasional misattribution and small transcription errors present (e.g., 'KV cash' vs 'KV cache', 'Redwood Dedciated' misspelling). Some timestamps are approximate.

End transcript.
